frameworks.name: The Home Position
frameworks.summary: A named, repeatable resting place for your hands that you return to after every gesture, so that your gesture vocabulary reads as deliberate rather than as nervous.
steps: Choose one default and write it down as a physical instruction, not a feeling - for example 'hands together at the belt buckle, fingers loosely overlapping' rather than 'relaxed'.

Set the four constraints and check your choice against all of them: above the waist, in front of the body or just outside the hip line, visible to the room and to a camera, and physically relaxed rather than clenched.
Rehearse the cycle, not just the position: gesture out, return home, pause. The return is what makes a gesture read as punctuation, so rehearse the return as carefully as the gesture.
Assign every object a single job - clicker advances slides, glass is set down before you begin, card carries three anchors and one number - and never let a prop become a surface for your nerves.
Stand still for sixty seconds in front of a mirror or a camera and count how many times your hands leave the home position and fail to return. That count is your baseline.
In the first two weeks, return to home position deliberately at the end of every sentence. After that it should happen without a thought.
frameworks.whenToUse: Use it in every talk, every pitch, and every high-stakes conversation - it is the cheapest habit in this module and it is invisible when it works. Skip the formal drill and just keep your hands in view during a one-on-one coffee conversation, where the technique would be heavy-handed.
frameworks.example: A founder arrives at a Series B partner meeting with his hands behind his back. He names the home position before the meeting - hands together at the belt buckle - and rehearses the gesture-return cycle three times in front of a hotel mirror. In the meeting, when the partner asks about churn, he gestures once with an open palm to mark the point and returns to the buckle. When the partner pushes back on the bridge, he does not clasp, does not touch his face, and does not put his hands in his pockets; he returns to the buckle, which reads as composed rather than as defensive. The partner later says, unprompted, that he 'did not seem to be selling'. The clicker never leaves his right hand, low and still.

frameworks.name: The Movement Map
frameworks.summary: A plan of three or four positions in a room, each assigned to a section of the talk, so that travel is authored by the content rather than generated by nerves.
steps: Draw the room before you rehearse: mark the screen, the front edge, the door, the table, the decision-maker's seat, and the audience's cluster positions.
Set three or four positions and no more - home centre, stage left, stage right, and one advance position a step closer to the audience - and mark them on the drawing.
Assign each position to a content section, in order. A position with no section attached will not be used on the day.
Define the trigger: the exact sentence that sends you to the next position, so the move happens at a thought boundary and never mid-sentence.
Define the plant - feet still, weight even, hips square - and rehearse the stop as carefully as the walk, because the stop is what makes the travel look deliberate.
Audit on a recording: count returns to the same spot inside a thirty-second window. More than two means you were pacing, and the room saw it.
frameworks.whenToUse: Use it for any talk longer than five minutes in a room you have not used before, and for any talk in a large space where staying still would read as a slide with legs. Do not use it for a five-minute item in a small meeting room, where the correct map is a seated triangle and no travel at all.
frameworks.example: A COO is asked to present a 12-minute reorganisation plan to her executive team in a 20-person boardroom. She draws the room: long table, screen on the short wall, the CEO at the head. Her map has three positions - standing at the foot of the table for the diagnosis, a step to the right for the cost analysis, and back to the foot for the recommendation - and one seated section for the discussion. The trigger for each move is a specific sentence she has written on her card. In the room, she moves exactly twice, each time planting before she speaks, and sits down for the discussion. Her VP later reports that the reorganisation 'felt calm, which is what I wanted'.

frameworks.name: The Triangle Scan
frameworks.summary: A gaze pattern that cycles through a person's eyes and mouth - or through three zones of a room - so that attention is distributed and never becomes a stare.
steps: In a one-on-one or a group of six or fewer, cycle the triangle: left eye, right eye, then mouth or forehead, holding the whole triangle for one completed thought before moving on.
In rooms of more than about a dozen people, define three zones - left, centre, right - and land fully on one zone per thought instead of sweeping continuously.
Hold each landing for one completed thought, roughly three to five seconds. Shorter reads as skimming; much longer reads as a challenge.
Answer to the room: hold the person who asked for the first sentence of your answer, then turn outward to the rest of the room for the substance, so the reply does not become a private exchange.
For your single most important line, choose one person whose eyes you can actually see and give the line to them. Pre-select that person in the room read.
Ban the three glances during key lines: the screen, your notes, and the ceiling. Pre-load the number so the eyes are already there when it is spoken.
frameworks.whenToUse: Use it in every room, and rehearse it specifically on a recording - it is nearly impossible to feel honest about your own eye contact. In a one-on-one with a known counterpart, deliberately moderate it: the same gaze that reads as attention in a pitch reads as pressure in a negotiation.
frameworks.example: A founder is recording a 3-minute investor update. On the first take she locks onto the camera lens for 40 seconds and never looks away. On the second take she applies the triangle: with a colleague in the room she cycles eye, eye, mouth for each thought, and for the one line that matters - the net revenue retention figure - she picks the CFO, who is visible on the right, and gives the line to her. The colleague's note afterwards: 'I stopped looking at the screen twice, which means the number landed.'

frameworks.name: The Plant-and-Pivot
frameworks.summary: A four-beat technique for changing which part of the room you are addressing - plant, pivot, pause, speak - that makes directed movement read as intention rather than as a hunt for something to look at.
steps: Plant: both feet down, weight even, hips square to the room, and the line under your shoulders level. Do this before you move, not as you move.
Pivot: turn from the hips so the torso rotates with the head, and let your gaze travel with the rotation to the new section. A head turn alone is ambiguous; a supported turn is not.
Pause: hold the new orientation for a beat. The pause is what announces the section change and stops the new content landing on top of the old.
Speak: deliver the first line of the new section from the plant, without moving, and keep the feet still until the section is finished.
Protect sightlines: never pivot so far that your back is to the room, never stand in front of the screen, and never stand over a seated colleague who needs to see both you and the slide.
Rehearse it in three contexts - a large stage, a boardroom table, and a small circle of seated peers - so the same four beats work in all three.
frameworks.whenToUse: Use it whenever you change who you are talking to: switching from a section of the room to another, handing the floor to a colleague, or turning to acknowledge a late arrival. Do not use it to turn towards the screen mid-sentence - use the pointer instead, or check the screen only at a thought boundary.
frameworks.example: A VP is presenting to a board of eleven when a director who missed the first item slips in late. The VP does not interrupt her sentence and does not gesture at the door. She finishes the sentence, plants, pivots 30 degrees toward the new arrival, pauses, and says, 'Good to have you with us, Marcus - we are on the third of five, and it is the unit economics.' Then she pivots back and continues. The pivot and the sentence take four seconds, and the board sees an acknowledgement rather than a disruption.

frameworks.name: The Gesture Checklist
frameworks.summary: A pre-talk audit that classifies your habitual movements, assigns each one a verdict, and produces a short list of deliberate gestures matched to specific lines.
steps: Record two minutes of yourself talking about your work with no preparation, and do not re-record it.

Log every movement by family: illustrators (maps onto content), emphatics (content-independent), regulators (controls the room), adaptors (self-directed and tension-managing), and dead hand (no movement at all).
For each adaptor, note the trigger - which words, which slides, which topic. Then delete the two that fire most often and redesign the moment that caused them.
Assign the emphatics: pick the two or three lines in your talk that must land, and give each exactly one emphatic. Everywhere else, no emphatic at all.
Choose at most two illustrators, at moments where a picture genuinely helps - a size, a shape, a direction - and rehearse them so they are recognisable and brief.
Write the one-line body plan on your card next to your three anchors: home position, movement map, eye-contact target for the key line, and the prop rule.
frameworks.whenToUse: Run it once before a talk that matters, and once a month on any real recorded material, so the list stays current as your content changes. It is most valuable on recordings rather than in your own memory, because self-assessment in the moment is systematically rosier than the tape.
frameworks.example: A founder's two-minute baseline shows 22 distinct hand movements, of which 14 are self-directed: four face touches, three cuff adjustments, two ring rotations, and five instances of picking up and putting down a pen. The two that fire most often both occur on the sentence about last quarter's revenue miss, so the redesign is structural: he moves the revenue slide to a 30-second section delivered from the plant with both hands in the home position, and he stops bringing the pen onto the podium. He assigns emphatics to exactly two sentences - the one about the number and the one about the ask - and the checklist becomes one line on his card: 'Home position, two emphatics, no pen, plant on the revenue slide.'

scenarios.title: The recorded investor pitch where you can see your own pacing
scenarios.setting: You have recorded yourself delivering a 4-minute Series A update and you have watched it back for the first time. The company is raising 8 million. The footage shows you moving back and forth across the frame continuously, and your chief of staff, watching beside you, says 'you look like you are waiting for something'.
scenarios.challenge: The argument is strong and the numbers are good. But in the recording you never stand still for longer than about four seconds, your hands have no home position, and on the sentence about gross margin you can see yourself pacing harder than anywhere else in the talk.
objectives: Diagnose the pacing as a design failure rather than as a nerves failure
Cut the number of positions from five to three and attach each to a content section
Establish a home position and return to it after every gesture

options.text: Re-record the talk, this time trying to stand perfectly still in one spot for the full four minutes.
options.outcome: You are now a slide with legs. The stillness reads as rigidity to anyone watching the video, and because you are fighting the urge to move, the delivery loses its energy and your gestures disappear entirely. You have replaced one legible tell with a worse one.
options.feedback: Stillness is not the opposite of pacing; it is a different symptom of the same problem, which is that movement is unowned. The fix is not zero movement - it is movement with an assigned reason. Three positions, three sections, and every move ends in a plant.

options.text: Keep the recording, log every movement by family, delete your two most frequent adaptors, assign emphatics to two specific lines, and draw a three-position movement map with a trigger sentence for each move.
options.outcome: The second take has four visible moves instead of thirty, each one at a thought boundary, and your hands return to the belt buckle between gestures. Your chief of staff's comment changes from 'you look like you are waiting for something' to 'you look like you are about to tell me something'.
options.feedback: This is the correct diagnosis. Note the second-order effect: because the movement is now authored, the energy that was leaking into pacing shows up in your delivery instead. Do the map in the actual room dimensions - a 4-minute pitch to investors is usually delivered standing at a table, not on a stage, and the map changes accordingly.

options.text: Cut the talk to 90 seconds, since the space between your points is where the pacing shows.
options.outcome: You have removed the visible symptom by removing the content, and you have also removed the two minutes in which the investors would have learned what you actually do. The short version is tighter and lands faster, but the decision you needed them to make is no longer supported by enough evidence.
options.feedback: Brevity is a legitimate fix for a rambling talk, but it is the wrong fix for a pacing problem. Tighten by removing the weakest section, not the pacing - and do the map either way, because the next talk will have the same habit.

options.text: Ask your chief of staff to film you at the next team meeting so you can get a second angle on the pacing.
options.outcome: A second angle is a reasonable diagnostic, but you have now spent the week gathering footage of a problem you can already see, and the habit will be reinforced in the meantime because nothing about it is changing.
options.feedback: Gathering more data on a problem you have already diagnosed is procrastination with a camera. You can see the pacing, you can see the missing home position, and you have a name for both. Act on the recording you have.

scenarios.coachingNote: Pacing is a design failure disguised as a nerves failure. The number of positions in a talk is a decision, not a symptom, and it can be set in advance. Count your returns to the same spot inside a thirty-second window on any recording; more than two means the room was watching you wander rather than listening.

scenarios.title: The boardroom where you are the only one standing
scenarios.setting: A quarterly board meeting. Ten directors around a long table. You are presenting the FY27 plan because the CEO asked you to. You are standing at the side of the room with a clicker, presenting to eleven seated people who are all at least fifteen years your senior.
scenarios.challenge: The CFO, seated opposite, has a laptop open and a proposal in front of him that contradicts your capital allocation. You have eight minutes, and the physical geometry is working against you: you are above them, they are below you, and you have no stage.
objectives: Use your standing position without turning it into a dominance display
Keep the geometry from making you the antagonist in the room
Deliver the capital allocation argument with your body supporting the words

options.text: Stand in the centre of the room behind the head chair, and hold the clicker up while you speak.
options.outcome: You have taken the position of the chair and made the room look like an audience at your performance. The directors, who are used to being the ones with power, register a subtle challenge, and the CFO's opposition hardens because your body has already positioned you against the table.
options.feedback: Geometry is a message. Standing behind the head chair claims the room's authority while the room keeps its decision rights, which reads as presumptuous. Move to the side, get a sightline to every face, and give the clicker a job.

options.text: Stand at the side of the room with a clear sightline to all eleven, deliver your eight minutes in three defined positions each tied to a section, and sit back down at the table for the discussion.
options.outcome: The directors get the argument without a performance, and returning to the table after the presentation makes clear that you are one of them reporting, not an outside party presenting at them. When the CFO raises his contradiction, the room is in a discussion rather than a confrontation.
options.feedback: Correct. The return to the chair is the part people skip, and it is what converts a status display into a report. Also plan the moment you sit: the pivot, the pause, and the hand-off - 'I will take questions now' - rehearsed, so that the transition looks like a plan rather than an awkward manoeuvre.

options.text: Stay seated and present from the chair like everyone else, using the screen for all of the material.
options.outcome: Peer-level, which is comfortable, but you now have to compete with a screen for attention and you have no way to signal emphasis except with your voice. For an eight-minute plan with a contested capital allocation, the room's attention slides to the CFO's laptop within about two minutes.
options.feedback: Sitting is defensible and often better in a small room - but only if you can hold attention another way. If you sit, stand only for the section where you need the room's full attention, and use your hands and gaze more deliberately, because you have removed the movement as a tool.

options.text: Hand the presentation to the CEO and let them present your numbers.
options.outcome: You have removed the physical problem by removing yourself, and you have also removed your credibility with the room. The CEO is now defending numbers they did not build, and your section becomes a document being read aloud. Any weakness in the plan is now the CEO's problem, which is exactly where you do not want it.
options.feedback: Never hand over the argument you were asked to make. If the geometry is wrong, fix the geometry - move to the side, shorten the presentation, sit down at the end. Handing over reads as avoidance or as being unwilling to be measured.

scenarios.coachingNote: Standing is a status display, and in a room where everyone else is seated it must be bounded. Stand to deliver, plant, and sit to discuss. The return to the table is what keeps the position from reading as dominance.

scenarios.title: The clicker that dies on the main stage
scenarios.setting: You are on a 400-person conference stage, 25 minutes in, at the moment of the slide that carries your most important number. Your clicker has been working for 20 minutes. Your chief of staff is in the wings. The AV technician is on the left side of the stage.
scenarios.challenge: The clicker fails. You press it and nothing happens, and the slide behind you is still the previous one, and the number the room needs is on the next slide.
objectives: Keep talking through the failure without a visible pause or a look at the ceiling
Recover the slide without abandoning your audience or your place on the stage
Turn an equipment failure into a moment that does not cost credibility

options.text: Stop, look up at the screen, press the clicker again, then say 'sorry, technical issue, one moment' and wait.
options.outcome: You have handed the room a problem to solve. The 400 people now have nothing to look at but you fumbling, and the pause has converted a technical problem into visible incompetence. Several people check their phones during the wait.
options.feedback: The worst version of this is the apology and the wait, because it tells the room the problem is now their responsibility. Cover the gap with the sentence you were already saying, and give them something to look at while you fix it.

options.text: Keep speaking - repeat the number aloud in the sentence you were in the middle of - walk to the screen, advance it manually, and continue from the new position without a comment on the failure.
options.outcome: The room heard the key number from you, which is what they came for, and they watched you solve a problem in real time without being asked to. A brief physical action in front of an audience is often read as confidence, not embarrassment.
options.feedback: This is the rehearsed version. Say the number out loud so the slide becomes reinforcement rather than the source. Walk deliberately - it is now legitimate movement - and plant before you resume. And always carry a backup: a presenter remote in the lectern, a second clicker in your pocket, or the deck on the screen in advance.

options.text: Signal the technician from the stage and continue presenting while they fix it.
options.outcome: You have handed the room a 400-person problem and a visible stoppage, and you have spent your most valuable moment - the one attached to your most important number - on logistics. The number is now less memorable, not more.
options.feedback: Do not pull the AV into your moment. Handling a small problem yourself is far cheaper than a 400-person visible stoppage. The technician is there for the equipment, not for the show.

options.text: Ask the room to imagine the chart while you describe it, and skip the slide entirely.
options.outcome: Sometimes correct, occasionally even stronger - the audience builds the picture with you. But used as a reflex after a failure, it is a retreat: you have just told the room that the visual evidence you had was optional.
options.feedback: A good instinct when the slide adds little, and a bad default when the slide carries the number they need. Decide before the talk which of your slides is essential; if the failure hits an essential slide, advance it manually. If it hits a decorative one, narrate and move on.

scenarios.coachingNote: Equipment failure is a stagecraft problem, not a composure test. Rehearse it once, badly, on purpose: cover the gap with speech, advance the slide, and never comment on the failure. The room forgives a dead clicker and never forgives the face that follows it.

scenarios.title: The five-minute item in a small meeting room
scenarios.setting: A 20-person leadership team in a 9x4 metre meeting room. There is no stage and no screen on a wall - the deck is on a laptop at one end. You have five minutes in a 60-minute meeting to present a proposal that is genuinely contested: the team thinks you are expanding scope.
scenarios.challenge: Everything in your stage instincts says to stand up, walk to the screen, and project. The room is small, half the people are at a table, and there is no front to stand at.
objectives: Match your physical register to a room with no stage and no front
Deliver a contested proposal without physically dominating it
Use your hands, gaze, and voice - not your altitude - to hold the room

options.text: Stand up, walk to the laptop, and present the slides from the front of the table.
options.outcome: You have blocked the line of sight of eight people, you have converted a five-minute team item into a performance, and the team reads the gesture as you needing the floor. A proposal that was already contested is now contested on two fronts.
options.feedback: Theatre in a small room is read as insecurity or as a bid for authority, and both cost you. Stay seated. Your tools in this room are your hands above the table edge, your gaze, and your voice - the room is close enough that the voice does more work than it would from a stage.

options.text: Stay seated, keep your hands visible above the table edge, drive the room with a deliberate gaze pattern, and stand only for the twenty seconds it takes to turn the laptop screen toward the group.
options.outcome: The room stays in conversation with you rather than in a presentation at you, and the twenty seconds of standing is clearly a tool rather than a stance. The proposal is still contested, but it is contested on its merits rather than on your body language.
options.feedback: Right, and the detail that makes it work is the seated hand position: visible above the table edge rather than in your lap, which is where most speakers put them and where the room loses you. Also name the single ask at the end - in a small room, the ask is what converts an item into a decision.

options.text: Sit at the table, skip the deck entirely, and make the case conversationally with one colleague who will back you.
options.outcome: Sound, if the colleague is credible and the room trusts them, but you have handed a third of your authority to someone else and you have removed the only visual anchor for your data. If the colleague hesitates, the room now has nothing to look at.
options.feedback: A good instinct in a small room - fewer artefacts, more conversation - but the collateral support weakens your position and loses your evidence. Present your own material, turn the screen briefly, and make the case in your own voice.

options.text: Send the proposal as a one-page document and offer to take questions afterwards instead of presenting.
options.outcome: You have removed the five minutes from the room's calendar and with them the only chance to make the argument. The document gets read - or does not - and the 'afterwards' becomes a scheduling negotiation that usually goes nowhere.
options.feedback: Do not substitute documentation for presence in a contested decision. A written proposal asks the room to do your work in private, at their own pace, without you in the room to answer the first question. The five minutes is the deliverable.

scenarios.coachingNote: Venue determines register, and the register is not a preference. A circle of seated peers gets a seated, conversational, contained body. A room with a front and a screen gets a standing, projected one. Copying conference stagecraft into a meeting room is the fastest way to look like an outsider in your own company.

scenarios.title: The counterparty whose hands never stop
scenarios.setting: You are in a term-sheet negotiation with the lead investor's operating partner, across a table, with your CFO beside you. You are presenting the round. Halfway through, she starts touching her neck and then the corner of her mouth, and she stops writing in her notebook.
scenarios.challenge: Your own body is composed, but hers is not, and you have to decide what that means - and what to do about it - without changing your own delivery in a way that makes the negotiation worse.
objectives: Read the behavioural cluster without over-claiming what it means
Avoid both the naive 'she is uncomfortable, I win' and the naive 'it is nothing'
Keep your own body congruent while you adjust what you say

options.text: Conclude that she is uncomfortable with the terms and press harder on the ask.
options.outcome: You have acted on a single inference from behaviour with a low base rate. If she was uncomfortable because the number is wrong, pressing hard damages the relationship you will need to close the round. Worse, you have changed your behaviour, and she will read the pressure as a sign that you are hiding something.
options.feedback: This is the base-rate error. Everyone touches their face; the signal is the change and the clustering, not the instance. And the meaning is ambiguous - discomfort, scepticism, disagreement, a thought about something else entirely. Change what you say, not how hard you press.

options.text: Slow down your own delivery, drop to a more concrete and specific part of the plan, and ask an open question about what matters most to her, while keeping your own posture settled and open.
options.outcome: You have done the only thing that is genuinely useful with an observed cluster: you have lowered the pressure and shifted the conversation toward her concerns. If the cluster was discomfort with a specific term, you will find out which one. Your settled body also makes it harder for her to read you as rattled.
options.feedback: This is the disciplined response. Change the conversation, not the volume of the ask, and let the cluster tell you what to ask about rather than telling you what to conclude. You can verify the signal by testing it - ask the open question and watch whether the behaviour stops or escalates.

options.text: Ask your CFO to take over the detail while you watch her body language.
options.outcome: You have outsourced the presentation and turned the negotiation into surveillance. It also removes your main conversational tool - your own attention - and the CFO is now presenting a plan to a partner who has stopped taking notes.
options.feedback: The instinct to reduce pressure is right; the handover is heavy-handed. If you want to lower the temperature, take a different tack yourself - a pause, a concession on a detail, or a direct question about what she is weighing.

options.text: Mirror her behaviour deliberately, matching her touch rate, so that you appear relaxed and in sync with her.
options.outcome: You have made your body a performance of relaxation while she is watching, and the mimicry is visible to anyone trained to spot it. It also leaves your own hands with nothing to do, because you are busy copying her.
options.feedback: Deliberate mirroring is theatre, and it makes your own behaviour less natural rather than more. If you want to lower the temperature, lower it vocally: slow down, soften, and ask a question. Your hands should be at home position, not busy.

scenarios.coachingNote: Observed behaviour is a weak single signal and a strong pattern signal. Never act on one instance; look for a change in rate or a cluster at the moment you named a number, a date, or a request. And when you see it, change the conversation rather than the pressure - the correct response to discomfort is usually a better question.

exercises.title: The gesture family audit
exercises.instructions: Record two minutes of yourself talking about your own work with no preparation and no re-recording. Then watch it at normal speed with a notebook, and log every movement you can see into one of five categories: illustrator (maps onto what you are saying), emphatic (marks emphasis, independent of content), regulator (controls the room - a hand lift to continue, a palm-down to slow down), adaptor (self-directed, tension-managing - face, cuff, ring, pen, hair), and dead hand (no movement at all across a stretch). For each adaptor, write the trigger word or the topic it clusters around. Then do a second two-minute recording with exactly three changes: the two most frequent adaptors deleted, the home position enforced between gestures, and emphatics assigned to no more than two sentences.
exercises.deliverable: Two two-minute recordings plus a one-page gesture log with counts by family, the trigger for each adaptor, and the three changes made in the second take.
successCriteria: The first recording is unedited, unrehearsed, and produced in a single take.

The log distinguishes the five families by function rather than by appearance - for example, the same hand lift is logged as a regulator in one place and an adaptor in another, with the reason stated.
The two most frequent adaptors are named, and the trigger for each is written down in words.
The second recording shows a visible return to a single home position between gestures, with no more than two emphatics in total.
The log identifies at least one dead-hand stretch longer than ten seconds in the first recording.
exercises.liveCoachPrompt: We are going to log your movements, not fix your content, so do not polish what you are saying. Two minutes, one take, then we go through it together and put every movement into one of five buckets. The interesting part is always the adaptors and what triggers them - usually one sentence of the talk accounts for most of them. By the end I want you to know your two worst habits and where they live, and I want your second take to be visibly calmer than your first.

exercises.title: Build the movement map for a real room
exercises.instructions: Pick a real talk you have coming in the next two weeks, in a room you have not used before. Walk the empty room if you can, or stand in the actual seat. Draw the room: screen, front edge, door, table, and where the decision-maker will sit. Mark three or four positions on the drawing and assign each one to a section of your talk, in order. Write the exact trigger sentence that sends you to each position, and specify the plant for each one - feet, weight, hips. Then rehearse the talk standing in the room, out loud, with a timer, and move only on your trigger sentences. Record one rehearsal. Afterwards, count the number of times you returned to the same spot inside a thirty-second window.
exercises.deliverable: A hand-drawn or drawn map of the room with positions, section assignments, trigger sentences, and plant specifications, plus a recorded rehearsal and the return-count figure.
successCriteria: The map has three or four positions, each attached to a named section of the talk, and each with a written trigger sentence.
Every position has a specified plant, and the rehearsal shows the plant happening before the first line of the new section.
The recorded rehearsal shows no move that occurs in the middle of a sentence.
The return-count figure is recorded honestly, and if it is above two in any thirty-second window you have identified which movement is generating it and changed the map.
The map reflects the actual geometry of the room, including the position of the screen and the door.
exercises.liveCoachPrompt: Before anything else I need the room: how big, where is the screen, where will the decision-maker sit, and is there a table. Then we will place three or four positions and write the trigger sentence for each, because the trigger is what stops the wandering. Go and stand in the room before you rehearse, because the map drawn at your desk is always wrong about where the space actually is.

exercises.title: The triangle scan rehearsal
exercises.instructions: Set up a phone at eye level with three people in the room at three different positions - left, centre, right - or with a colleague and a wall chart if you are alone. Deliver a 90-second explanation of a real project. Take one take. Watch it and mark every point where your gaze landed and held for less than a second, and every point where it stayed on one person for more than five seconds. Take a second take applying the triangle scan: land fully on one zone for one completed thought, then move; and for your single most important sentence, pre-select one person whose eyes you can see and give the line to them. Take a third take with the same rule and a slower pace. Compare the three.
exercises.deliverable: Three 90-second recordings and a one-page comparison of gaze pattern across the three, with a marked count of short landings and long holds in each.
successCriteria: Take one shows a consistent pattern of short landings or a long hold on a single person, and the comparison identifies which.
In take two, each landing is held for a full thought and the count of sub-second landings is visibly lower.
The most important sentence is delivered to a pre-selected named person in takes two and three, with the eyes already there when the line starts.
The speaker does not look at the screen, notes, or ceiling during the key line in any take.
The written comparison states which take would actually be delivered live, and why.
exercises.liveCoachPrompt: Three takes of the same ninety seconds, and we are only changing your eyes. The rule is simple: land on one person for one complete thought, then release, and give your most important line to one face you chose in advance. After the takes, tell me which one felt worse and which one looked better, because that gap is the whole exercise - your internal sense of eye contact is not a reliable instrument.

exercises.title: The five-minute item, seated, in a small room
exercises.instructions: Find a real meeting in the next week with a small group - six to twelve people, ideally around a table - where you have an item. Decide in advance that you will stay seated for the entire item, and that your hands will be visible above the table edge the whole time, never in your lap and never in your pockets. Deliver your item without standing. Afterwards, write three lines: what the room's response was, whether you caught yourself with your hands out of sight, and whether standing would have actually helped - and if so, why. Then, as a second part, find a moment in the same meeting where the topic turns difficult, and plant your feet deliberately and keep your body level through it, and note how that felt and how it read.
exercises.deliverable: The delivered item, plus a five-line written note on the seated register, the visibility of your hands, and the physical choice you made at the hard moment.
successCriteria: The entire item was delivered seated, with no standing except to turn a screen if a screen was needed.
Your hands were visible above the table edge for the whole item, and you note honestly how often they were not.
You describe one concrete physical choice you made at the difficult moment and what you observed in response.
The note distinguishes between 'standing would have been more visible' and 'standing would have changed the power relationship', and only one of those is usually true.
The item ended with a clear, specific ask delivered from a settled posture.
exercises.liveCoachPrompt: This one is about restraint, which is harder than it sounds. Stay in your chair for the whole item, and keep your hands where the room can see them - that last part is the thing people miss. The second half matters more: when the conversation turns to the part they disagree with, plant your feet and keep your body level, and then tell me what you observed in their faces when you did.

exercises.title: The plant-and-pivot drill in three venues
exercises.instructions: Rehearse the same 60-second section three times, in three venues: a large room where you can walk, a boardroom with a long table and seated people, and a small circle of six colleagues. In each, change your address three times using plant-and-pivot: plant both feet with weight even, pivot from the hips to the new section, pause for a beat, then speak the first line without moving. Record all three. Then have a colleague or a camera assess one question per venue: does the turn read as intention, or as searching for something? In the boardroom version, you must also sit down at the end and stay seated - rehearse the hand-off line. Finally, on a stage or in a large room, deliberately kill your clicker mid-rehearsal and recover it: cover the gap by speaking the number aloud, walk to the screen, advance manually, and resume from the new position without commenting on the failure.
exercises.deliverable: Three 60-second recordings, one per venue, plus a written note on how the pivot reads in each and a rehearsed description of the dead-clicker recovery.
successCriteria: All three venue versions use the same four beats - plant, pivot, pause, speak - and the pause is visible in the recording.
The feet do not shuffle or shift weight during any pivot; the hips lead the turn.
The boardroom version ends with the speaker seated and the hand-off line delivered without a pause.
The dead-clicker recovery is completed without a look at the ceiling, an apology, or a break in speech.
The written note identifies which venue produced the most natural pivot and explains why the other two felt more effortful.
exercises.liveCoachPrompt: Same sixty seconds, three rooms, one technique: plant, pivot, pause, then speak. The order matters - if you talk through the pivot, the turn reads as a hunt for your words. Do the boardroom version last, and finish it by sitting down, because sitting down is part of the technique. We will also kill the clicker on purpose at some point, so that the failure is a rehearsed move rather than a surprise.

exercises.title: The body audit on a real recorded talk
exercises.instructions: Take the most recent recorded talk of any length that was not a rehearsal - a real meeting, a real presentation, a real pitch. Watch it at 1.5x with a pen and produce four counts: the number of distinct hand positions, the number of returns to the same spot inside a thirty-second window, the longest stretch of complete stillness, and the number of times you turned away from the audience or looked at a screen or notes. Then watch a second time, at normal speed, and mark every moment your body contradicted your words - the classic ones are a bright tone with a collapsed posture, or a confident claim with a shrinking gesture. Write down the three moments that were most incongruent, and for each one, say whether the body was right and the words were wrong, or the words were right and the body was wrong.
exercises.deliverable: A one-page audit with the four counts, the three incongruent moments with timestamps, and a verdict for each one on whether the body or the words were wrong.
successCriteria: All four counts are from the recording, not estimated, and one of them surprises the speaker.
At least three incongruent moments are identified with timestamps, and each gets a verdict.
At least one verdict concludes that the body was right and the words needed changing.
The audit names one specific change for the next talk rather than a general intention to be calmer.
The return-count figure is compared against the threshold of two per thirty seconds, and a conclusion is drawn.
exercises.liveCoachPrompt: This is a forensic exercise, so bring the recording and expect the counts to be slightly worse than your memory. Four numbers, then three specific moments where your body and your words disagreed, and for each one we decide which of the two was lying. The verdict matters more than the count - especially the moment where the body was right.

exercises.title: Write your one-page body plan
exercises.instructions: Write a single page that governs your body in every talk from now on. It must contain six fields: (1) your home position, written as a physical instruction; (2) your two most frequent adaptors, and the redesign for each; (3) the two lines in a talk that carry an emphatic, and the rule that nowhere else does; (4) the prop rule - what is in your hand, what job it does, and where it goes when it is not doing that job; (5) the eye-contact rule, including who you pick for the key line; (6) the movement rule, including the plant and the rule against moving during a key line. Underneath, add a one-line pre-stage checklist you can run in 30 seconds. Then find a talk in the next two weeks and put the six fields on a single index card, and keep the card in the room with you for that talk.
exercises.deliverable: A completed one-page body plan with all six fields, a 30-second pre-stage checklist, and the index card prepared for a real upcoming talk.
successCriteria: All six fields are present, specific, and written as instructions rather than intentions.
The home position is described in physical terms - for example, 'hands together at the belt buckle' - and not as a feeling.
The two adaptors named are the two that actually appear most often in the gesture audit, and each has a concrete redesign.
The pre-stage checklist can be run in under 30 seconds and contains no step that requires thought.
The index card for a real upcoming talk has been printed or written and carries all six fields in abbreviated form.
exercises.liveCoachPrompt: One page, six fields, and it has to work in every room you speak in, not just the one you are thinking of. The test is whether someone else could read it and know exactly what to do with their hands. Give me your two worst adaptors and the two sentences that matter most in a typical talk, and we will write the rest together - then you take it into a real room this month and tell me which field you actually used.

assessment.title: The live presence audit
assessment.brief: You will deliver a 7-minute segment on a topic you genuinely need a decision on, in a venue you have not used before, and you will be assessed on what the room sees as well as what it hears. Before the session you submit your movement map for that room, your one-page Gesture Checklist, and a 90-second baseline recording. On the day, the panel is seated in three clusters, one of which is two minutes late and enters during your third section. You are given a clicker and a slide deck with a mid-deck failure point. A talk with a superb argument and a restless body, or a calm body and no argument, both fail this assessment.

rubric.excellent: A named home position is evident throughout and the speaker returns to it after every gesture, so that gestures read as deliberate punctuation. Illustrators appear only where a picture genuinely helps, emphatics land on the two or three key phrases and no others, and there are no repeated self-directed adaptors - no face-touching, cuff-adjusting, or object-fiddling clusters. The prop in hand is used for one job and stays at rest between uses.
rubric.adequate: Gestures are present and broadly appropriate, but the hands have no settled default: they drift between several positions, and at least one nervous habit recurs, usually around the highest-stakes number. Emphasis lands more often than it should, so the key phrases lose their distinctiveness. A prop is used for a second job, such as pointing with a clicker or reading a card.
rubric.poor: The hands are either dead - pinned to the sides, clasped, or hidden - or continuously busy with a single repeated adaptor. Gesture and emphasis are indistinguishable, so nothing is marked. A prop is read from verbatim, or the speaker is visibly performing a pose the body does not support.

rubric.excellent: The speaker occupies three or four defined positions, each tied to a content section, and every move ends in a planted stance before the next section begins. Travel is slow, direct, and crossed at a diagonal rather than laterally. The speaker never crosses in front of the screen or turns their back to the room. On inspection, there is no pattern of repeated returns to the same spot inside a thirty-second window - there is no pacing.
rubric.adequate: The speaker uses the space and is not frozen, but the movement is loosely connected to the argument: one or two moves happen for no reason, one move occurs mid-sentence, and the speaker sometimes turns toward the screen to check it. Returns to the same position inside a thirty-second window occur, and read more as nervous energy than as intention.
rubric.poor: The speaker paces - a repetitive lateral or forward-back pattern, with no clear stop points - or does not move at all. Movement repeatedly coincides with the delivery of key lines, or the speaker's back is turned to the room during an important section.

rubric.excellent: Gaze lands and holds for one completed thought on a named person or a defined zone, then releases, in a consistent pattern across all three audience clusters. A deliberate choice of audience for the single most important line is visible. When the panelist arrives late, the speaker acknowledges them with a brief look and a sentence, then returns to the argument. There is no sustained lock on a single person and no continuous scanning.
rubric.adequate: Contact is made and mostly sustained, but the pattern is inconsistent: the speaker holds some people too long, drops others entirely, or looks at the screen or the ceiling during at least one key sentence. Late arrival is handled without a stall, but not with any deliberate signal of acknowledgement.
rubric.poor: The speaker avoids eye contact - reading notes, the screen, or the floor for most of the talk - or fixes a stare on one person, most often the decision-maker, for extended stretches. Late arrival causes a visible derailment.

rubric.excellent: Baseline posture is settled, open, and stable, with the chest available and the hands visible; it is relaxed rather than rigid, and it varies deliberately with content - a still, level body for a hard number, an expansion for a positive turn. Body and words agree throughout, including at the point where the material turns difficult. The speaker does not repeat posture claims the evidence does not support.
rubric.adequate: Posture is generally consistent and open enough to read, but it is somewhat rigid, or it stays unchanged through every section, including the one where the message is hard. One point of body-word incongruence is visible, usually around an awkward number or an unwelcome transition.
rubric.poor: Posture is closed, collapsed, or theatrical - arms folded, shoulders rounded, weight on one hip, or a held power stance that reads as aggressive. Body and words visibly conflict, and the room can be seen discounting the words.

rubric.dimension: Stagecraft and adaptation to the venue
rubric.excellent: The physical register matches the room precisely - seated and contained if the room is a circle, standing and defined if the room expects a presentation, no theatre in either case. Sightlines are protected: nobody is stood over, nobody is blocked from the screen, and the front edge is respected. The clicker failure at the scripted point is covered without a pause, a look at the ceiling, or a drop in composure, and the speaker's hands, feet, and position are all visibly under control while it happens.
rubric.adequate: The register is broadly appropriate but slightly off - a hint of stage energy in a small room, or a bit flat in a room that needed lift. The equipment failure produces a visible, brief hesitation that is recovered from. Sightlines are mostly protected, with one minor obstruction.
rubric.poor: The delivery is transplanted from a conference stage into a room that does not want it, or vice versa: the speaker dominates a small table, or under-performs in a large venue. The equipment failure visibly breaks composure, and the speaker spends the recovery looking at the ceiling or at the back of the room.

rubric.dimension: Calibration: evidence-based choices and self-assessment accuracy
rubric.excellent: The submitted movement map, Gesture Checklist, and baseline recording show a specific diagnosis of the speaker's own behaviour, anchored to timestamps or named habits, and the delivered talk visibly implements the chosen changes. The speaker's self-assessment matches what the recording shows. Where the speaker describes a research claim, the scope is stated accurately - for example, 7-38-55 is described as a narrow decoding finding rather than a general law, and posture claims are not overstated.
rubric.adequate: The preparation artefacts exist and are reasonable, but the diagnosis is generic - 'I was nervous' rather than three named, observable behaviours - and only some of the changes are visible in the delivery. The self-assessment is broadly honest but misses at least one behaviour the recording clearly shows.
rubric.poor: There is no real diagnosis, or the submitted artefacts do not match the delivery. The speaker attributes the result to nerves or charisma rather than to specific behaviour, overstates what body-language research supports, or believes a change landed that the recording shows did not.

readingList.title: Nonverbal Communication in Human Interaction
readingList.author: Knapp, Hall, and Cooley
readingList.why: The standard academic reference for the field's vocabulary - kinesics, proxemics, regulators, adaptors, and the display rules - with a much more sceptical eye than the popular books. Pairs directly with the research-calibration concept in m06 and with the room-dynamics material in m10.

readingList.title: The Magic of Body Language
readingList.author: Eva Siegel
readingList.why: The classic practical treatment of body mapping - matching a physical movement to a specific meaning - and the origin of much of the coaching vocabulary in use today. Pairs with the movement map and the gesture checklist. Read it as a craft manual rather than as a scientific claim, because it is confident where the research is not.

readingList.title: What Every BODY Is Saying
readingList.author: Joe Navarro
readingList.why: A former FBI agent's field guide to behaviour clusters - especially the way several small behaviours read together rather than one behaviour alone. Directly useful for the adaptor-cluster and base-rate argument in m06, and for reading a counterparty across a table.

readingList.title: Resonate
readingList.author: Nancy Duarte
readingList.why: The best current treatment of how a speaker's physical presence and spatial language serve the argument, including the 'what is' versus 'what could be' structure and the idea of carrying an audience across a line. Pairs with the plant-and-pivot and stagecraft material in m06 and with the persuasion frameworks in m08.

readingList.title: The Speaker's Guidebook: Making Words Come Alive
readingList.author: Judith Weston
readingList.why: The most usable book on stagecraft for non-theatre audiences - movement, stance, gesture design, and how to rehearse the physical layer of a talk rather than only the words. Pairs with the home position, the movement map, and the recorded exercises in m06.

readingList.title: How Emotions Are Made
readingList.author: Lisa Feldman Barrett
readingList.why: The scientific case against universal facial expression decoding, and the read on Ekman's legacy that a sophisticated audience may know. Pairs with the research-calibration concept in m06 and with the credibility work in m01 - use it to check your own citations before someone else does.

masteryChecklist: I can state the scope of Mehrabian's 7-38-55 finding accurately in one sentence, and explain why it does not license the claim that my body overrides my words.
I can classify my own habitual gestures into illustrators, emphatics, regulators, and adaptors, and name the three adaptors I am going to eliminate.
I can hold a named home position - above the waist, visible, repeatable - and return to it after every gesture without thinking about it.
I can build a movement map for an unfamiliar room in ten minutes, with three or four positions each tied to a section of the talk.
I can execute plant-and-pivot without shuffling, and I can tell the difference between a pivot and a turn of the head in a recorded clip.
I can run the Triangle Scan and the three-second thought rule, and I can tell scanning apart from staring on a recording.
I can adjust my physical register to a boardroom, a small meeting room, and a conference stage without thinking about it, and I have a rehearsed plan for the dead clicker.
